topic: what an instruction is made of
prompt: An instruction is usually made up of a combination of an operation code and:

options.text: Some way of specifying an operand, most commonly by its location or address in memory
The number of cycles it will take
The address of the next instruction

explanation: Opcode plus a way of specifying an operand, usually by its location or address in memory. That is the whole shape of an instruction.

why.a: Correct. Opcode plus a way of specifying an operand, usually by its location or address in memory.
why.b: Wrong. Cycle counts are never encoded in an instruction.
why.c: Wrong. No checksum appears in any instruction format in this course.
why.d: Wrong. The program counter supplies the next address, except when a branch overrides it.

topic: what an instruction is made of
prompt: An operand is most commonly specified by its location or {{1}} in memory.
explanation: Address. Immediate addressing is the exception that proves the rule: there the value itself sits inside the instruction.

prompt: Instruction Format is defined as:

options.text: The layout of bits in an instruction
The order in which instructions execute
The set of instructions a processor supports
The way operands are accessed at runtime

explanation: The layout of bits in an instruction, for example the pattern 11100011111110000001110000 standing for ADD R1,R2.

why.a: Correct. The layout of bits in an instruction, for example the pattern 11100011111110000001110000 standing for ADD R1,R2.
why.b: Wrong. Execution order is program flow, not format.
why.c: Wrong. That is the instruction set.
why.d: Wrong. That is the addressing modes.

prompt: The deck gives 11100011111110000001110000 as an example of the bit layout for ADD R1,R2.
explanation: It does, and the point of showing it is that an assembly mnemonic is only a readable name for a pattern of bits.

why.true: Correct. The bit string appears on the instruction format slide against ADD R1,R2.
why.false: Wrong. The example is printed on the slide, immediately under the definition.

prompt: An instruction is divided into which parts?
explanation: Three parts. Note implicit or explicit against the operands: a zero-address instruction has operands, they are just implied by the stack.

why.a: Correct, and function is the deck's gloss on opcode.
why.b: Correct, and implicit operands are what make one-address and zero-address formats possible.
why.c: Correct, the addressing mode is the third part.
why.d: Wrong. The condition code register is read by branch instructions but is not a field of an instruction.

prompt: An instruction is divided into opcode, operands, which may be {{1}} or explicit, and addressing mode.
explanation: Implicit. The accumulator in a one-address instruction is the clearest case: it is an operand nobody writes down.

prompt: Instructions typically have how many operands?
explanation: 0, 1, 2 or 3, which is exactly why the deck goes on to work the same expression through four address formats.

why.a: Correct, and zero is on the list because of stack machines.
why.b: Wrong. Zero-address instructions exist, and the deck devotes three slides to them.
why.c: Wrong, though two-address instructions are the most common in commercial computers.
why.d: Wrong. The deck stops at 3.

prompt: There is usually more than one instruction format in an instruction set.
explanation: There usually is. Different instructions need different fields, so one fixed layout would waste bits on most of them.

why.true: Correct. The deck says so directly.
why.false: Wrong. A single format for every instruction is the exception, not the rule.

prompt: The bits of an instruction are divided into groups called:
explanation: Fields. Blocks and words are memory units, and segments are pipeline stages in this course, so the word matters.

why.a: Correct. Fields.
why.b: Wrong. A block is a group of words in memory, from the cache topic.
why.c: Wrong. A word is one or more complete rows of memory.
why.d: Wrong. Segment is the word the pipelining deck uses for a stage.

prompt: The format of an instruction is usually depicted in a {{1}} box symbolizing the bits of the instruction as they appear in memory words or in a control register.
explanation: Rectangular, with each field drawn as a slice of it. That drawing convention is why exam questions can ask for field widths in bits.

prompt: Select the most common fields found in instruction formats.
explanation: Three fields: Opcode, Mode, Address or Operand. The same three appear on the revision slide.

why.a: Correct, the opcode field specifies the operation.
why.b: Correct, the mode field says how the effective address is determined.
why.c: Correct, and the deck writes it as one field with two names.
why.d: Wrong. Length is not a field; in a variable-length format the opcode implies it.

prompt: Match each of the three common instruction fields to its position in the deck's general structure.
explanation: Opcode, Mode, Address. The order is worth holding because the address is always last, which is what lets an address field be widened without disturbing the opcode.

prompt: Match each instruction field to what it specifies.

pairs.right: A memory address or a processor register
The way the operand or the effective address is determined

explanation: Three fields, three jobs. Note that the address field can designate a register, not only memory, which is what makes register addressing fit the same layout.

prompt: The mode field of an instruction specifies:

options.text: The way the operand or the effective address is determined
A memory address or a processor register

explanation: How the operand is reached. It is the addressing mode written into the instruction itself.

why.a: Correct. How the operand is reached.
why.b: Wrong. That is the operation code field.
why.c: Wrong. That is the address field.
why.d: Wrong. Privilege levels are not covered in this course.

prompt: In the simple 16-bit instruction format example, what are the three field widths?

options.text: Opcode 4 bits, Register 4 bits, Address 8 bits
Opcode 8 bits, Register 4 bits, Address 4 bits
Opcode 4 bits, Register 8 bits, Address 4 bits
Opcode 6 bits, Register 4 bits, Address 6 bits

explanation: 4 plus 4 plus 8 is 16. The address takes half the instruction, which is typical: addresses need more bits than opcodes.

why.a: Correct. 4 plus 4 plus 8 is 16.
why.b: Wrong, and it reverses opcode and address.
why.c: Wrong. A register field of 8 bits would allow 256 registers, far more than the format implies.
why.d: Wrong. The widths given are 4, 4 and 8.

prompt: In the 16-bit format example the Address field is {{1}} bits wide.
explanation: 8 bits, so it can name 256 memory locations. That is what makes 11001010 read as location 202 in the binary example.

prompt: In the 16-bit format example, what does the 4-bit Register field specify?

options.text: A register, for example R1 or R2
The operation, for example ADD or SUB

explanation: A register, and with four bits it can name sixteen of them.

why.a: Correct. A register, and with four bits it can name sixteen of them.
why.b: Wrong. The operation comes from the opcode field, which is also 4 bits.
why.c: Wrong. That is the address field.
why.d: Wrong. This particular example has no separate mode field.

prompt: In the 16-bit format, the {{1}}-bit opcode defines the operation and the 8-bit field gives the {{2}} location.
explanation: A 4-bit opcode and an 8-bit memory address. Four bits of opcode allow sixteen distinct operations, which is the opcode-space trade-off in miniature.

prompt: The binary instruction 1010 0011 11001010 is interpreted as:
explanation: Opcode 1010 is ADD, register 0011 is R3, and address 11001010 is 202.

why.a: Correct. Opcode 1010 is ADD, register 0011 is R3, and address 11001010 is 202.
why.b: Wrong. 11001010 is 128 plus 64 plus 8 plus 2, which is 202.
why.c: Wrong. The opcode 1010 stands for ADD in this example.
why.d: Wrong. The register field 0011 is 3, not 10; 1010 is the opcode.

prompt: In the binary example the address field 11001010 is memory location {{1}}.
explanation: 202. Check it: 128 plus 64 plus 8 plus 2.

prompt: The 32-bit instruction 000001 00001 00010 00011 00000000000 is interpreted as:
explanation: Opcode 000001 is ADD, then R1 as the destination, R2 as operand 1 and R3 as operand 2.

why.a: Correct, and it is a three-address instruction, hence three register fields.
why.b: Wrong. The first register field after the opcode is the destination, and it holds 00001, which is R1.
why.c: Wrong. The opcode given for ADD is 000001.
why.d: Wrong. Three register fields are present, so it is a three-operand instruction.

prompt: In the 32-bit example the field 00001 is R1, the {{1}}, and the field 00011 is R3, {{2}}.
explanation: Destination first, then operand 1, then operand 2. The eleven trailing zeros are unused in this instruction.

prompt: Which expression does the deck use to compare the 3, 2, 1 and 0 address instruction formats?

options.text: X equals A plus B, times C plus D
X equals A times B, plus C times D
X equals A plus B plus C plus D
X equals A minus B, times C minus D

explanation: X equals A plus B, all times C plus D. Two additions and one multiplication, which is enough to show the difference between the formats without becoming long.

why.a: Correct. X equals A plus B, all times C plus D.
why.b: Wrong, and it swaps the operations round.
why.c: Wrong. There is a multiplication in the expression.
why.d: Wrong. Both inner operations are additions.

prompt: The same program is written in {{1}} different address formats to compare them.

blanks.hint: three, two, one and zero address

explanation: Four: three-address, two-address, one-address and zero-address.

prompt: How many instructions does the three-address program for X equals A plus B, times C plus D take?
explanation: Three: ADD R1, A, B then ADD R2, C, D then MUL X, R1, R2. That shortness is the format's stated advantage.

why.a: Correct. Three: ADD R1, A, B then ADD R2, C, D then MUL X, R1, R2.
why.b: Wrong. Six is the two-address program.
why.c: Wrong. Seven is the one-address program.
why.d: Wrong. Eight is the zero-address program.

prompt: In the three-address program the symbol M[A] denotes the {{1}} at the memory address symbolized by A.
explanation: Operand. The notation matters, because M[A] is the value stored at A, not A itself.

prompt: What is the disadvantage of the three-address format?

options.text: The binary-coded instructions require too many bits to specify three addresses
The programs are longer than in any other format

explanation: Too many bits per instruction. It is the classic trade: fewer instructions, but each one is larger.

why.a: Correct. Too many bits per instruction.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed: the advantage is that it results in short programs.
why.c: Wrong. The stack belongs to the zero-address format.
why.d: Wrong. The worked program uses R1 and R2 throughout.

prompt: The advantage of the three-address format is that it results in short programs when evaluating arithmetic expressions.
explanation: It does, and the worked example proves it: three instructions against eight for the stack machine.

why.true: Correct. Short programs when evaluating arithmetic expressions is the deck's phrase.
why.false: Wrong. That is the stated advantage; the disadvantage is the number of bits each instruction needs.

prompt: Two-address instructions are described as:

options.text: The most common in commercial computers
The rarest of the four formats
Used only where there is no accumulator

explanation: The most common in commercial computers, and each address field can specify either a processor register or a memory word.

why.a: Correct. The most common in commercial computers, and each address field can specify either a processor register or a memory word.
why.b: Wrong. It is the most common, not the rarest.
why.c: Wrong. Stack machines use the zero-address format.
why.d: Wrong. The accumulator belongs to the one-address format.

prompt: In the two-address format each address field can specify either a processor register or a memory {{1}}.
explanation: Memory word. Blocks, pages and lines all belong to the memory hierarchy topic, not to instruction formats.

prompt: How many instructions does the two-address program for X equals A plus B, times C plus D take?
explanation: Six: MOV R1, A then ADD R1, B then MOV R2, C then ADD R2, D then MOL R1, R2 then MOV X, R1.

why.a: Correct. Six: MOV R1, A then ADD R1, B then MOV R2, C then ADD R2, D then MOL R1, R2 then MOV X, R1.
why.b: Wrong. Three is the three-address program.
why.c: Wrong. Seven is the one-address program.
why.d: Wrong. Eight is the zero-address program.

prompt: The two-address program opens with MOV R1, A then {{1}} R1, B, and closes with MOV X, {{2}}.
explanation: ADD R1, B, and the last instruction is MOV X, R1. R1 accumulates the whole result, which is why it is the register written out at the end.

prompt: In a two-address instruction, the first symbol listed is assumed to be:

options.text: Both a source and the destination where the result is transferred

explanation: Both at once. That convention is what makes two addresses enough for an operation that logically needs three.

why.a: Correct, and it is the reason ADD R1, B overwrites R1.
why.b: Wrong. If it were only a source, the result would have nowhere to go.
why.c: Wrong. It is read as well as written.
why.d: Wrong. The opcode is the mnemonic in front of the operands.

prompt: The MOV instruction moves or {{1}} the operands to and from memory and processor registers.
explanation: Transfers. Like all data movement, it copies: the source is unchanged, only the destination is written.

prompt: One-address instructions use an implied register for all data manipulation. Which one?
explanation: The accumulator. Because it is implied, it never has to be named in the instruction, which is what leaves room for only one address.

why.a: Correct. The accumulator.
why.b: Wrong. The PC holds the address of the next instruction.
why.c: Wrong. The IR holds the instruction being executed.
why.d: Wrong. The MAR holds the address of the memory location being accessed.

prompt: For multiplication and division in a one-address machine there is a need for a second register.
explanation: There is, and the deck then says it will neglect the second register and assume the AC contains the result of all operations, to keep the worked program simple.

why.true: Correct. A product can be twice as wide as its operands, which is why a second register is needed.
why.false: Wrong. The deck states the need and then sets it aside for the sake of the example.

prompt: How many instructions does the one-address program for X equals A plus B, times C plus D take?
explanation: Seven: LOAD A, ADD B, STORE T, LOAD C, ADD D, MOL T, STORE X.

why.a: Correct. Seven: LOAD A, ADD B, STORE T, LOAD C, ADD D, MOL T, STORE X.
why.b: Wrong. Six is the two-address program.
why.c: Wrong. Three is the three-address program.
why.d: Wrong. Eight is the zero-address program.

prompt: The one-address program begins {{1}} A, then ADD B, then STORE T.
explanation: LOAD. In a one-address machine the accumulator has to be filled before anything can be done to it.

prompt: In the one-address program, what is T?

options.text: The address of a temporary memory location for storing the intermediate result
The destination of the final result

explanation: A temporary memory location. With only one accumulator, the first sub-result has to be parked somewhere while the second is computed.

why.a: Correct. A temporary memory location.
why.b: Wrong. The deck explicitly neglects the second register in this example.
why.c: Wrong. TOS, the top of stack, belongs to the zero-address program.
why.d: Wrong. The final result goes to X.

prompt: In the one-address format all operations are done between the AC register and a memory operand.
explanation: They are, and that is the defining constraint: one operand is always the accumulator, so only the other needs an address.

why.true: Correct. The AC and one memory operand, every time.
why.false: Wrong. This is exactly how the deck describes the one-address format.

prompt: In a stack-organized computer, which instructions still need an address field?
explanation: PUSH and POP need an address to say which operand communicates with the stack. ADD and MUL take their operands from the top of the stack, so they need none.

why.a: Correct. PUSH and POP need an address to say which operand communicates with the stack.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed: these are the ones that use no address field.
why.c: Wrong. If all of them needed one, it would not be a zero-address machine.
why.d: Wrong. The stack has to be filled from somewhere, and PUSH is how.

prompt: A stack-organized computer does not use an address field for the instructions ADD and {{1}}.
explanation: MUL. Both take their operands from the top of the stack, so there is nothing to name.

prompt: How many instructions does the zero-address program for X equals A plus B, times C plus D take?
explanation: Eight: PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD, PUSH C, PUSH D, ADD, MOL, POP X. It is the longest of the four programs, which is the cost of carrying no addresses.

why.a: Correct. Eight: PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD, PUSH C, PUSH D, ADD, MOL, POP X.
why.b: Wrong. Seven is the one-address program.
why.c: Wrong. Six is the two-address program.
why.d: Wrong. Three is the three-address program.

prompt: In the zero-address program, {{1}} stands for top of stack.
explanation: TOS. The deck's comments track it line by line, so you can see the operands stack up and then collapse.

prompt: To evaluate arithmetic expressions in a stack computer, it is necessary to convert the expression into:
explanation: Reverse Polish notation, where the operator follows its operands. That is exactly the order the PUSH, PUSH, ADD sequence takes.

why.a: Correct. Reverse Polish notation, where the operator follows its operands.
why.b: Wrong. Scientific notation belongs to floating point.
why.c: Wrong. Two's complement is a way of writing negative integers.
why.d: Wrong. BCD codes decimal digits.

prompt: A stack computer can evaluate an arithmetic expression directly, without converting it to reverse Polish notation first.
explanation: The deck says the conversion is necessary. The stack has no way of holding a pending operator, so the operands must arrive before the operator does.

why.true: Wrong. The deck says it is necessary to convert the expression into reverse Polish notation.
why.false: Correct. The conversion is required, which is why the worked program pushes both operands before each ADD.

prompt: Why is this type of computer called zero-address?

options.text: Because of the absence of an address field in the computational instructions
Because it has no memory addresses at all
Because the stack always starts at address zero
Because every operand is at address zero

explanation: The computational instructions carry no address field. PUSH and POP still do, which is why the name is qualified in exactly that way.

why.a: Correct, and computational is the word that keeps the claim true.
why.b: Wrong. PUSH A names an address.
why.c: Wrong. Nothing in the deck fixes the stack at address zero.
why.d: Wrong. The operands are at their own addresses; they are simply not named in ADD or MUL.

prompt: The name zero-address is given because of the absence of an address field in the {{1}} instructions.
explanation: Computational. PUSH and POP are not computational, and they keep their address fields.

prompt: The revision class repeats that an instruction is divided into:
explanation: The same three parts as the ISA deck, along with the reminder that instructions typically have 0, 1, 2 or 3 operands.

why.a: Correct. The same three parts as the ISA deck, along with the reminder that instructions typically have 0, 1, 2 or 3 operands.
why.b: Wrong. The addressing mode is a third part.
why.c: Wrong. The condition code register is not part of an instruction.
why.d: Wrong. These are places operands can live, not the parts of an instruction.

prompt: The revision class repeats that the most common fields found in instruction formats are:

options.text: Opcode, Mode, and Address or Operand

explanation: The same three fields as the ISA deck. The other two options are real three-part layouts from elsewhere in the course, which is what makes them tempting.

why.a: Correct. The same three fields as the ISA deck.
why.b: Wrong. Register is a field in one worked example, not one of the three general fields.
why.c: Wrong. Tag, Index and Offset is the direct mapping cache address format.
why.d: Wrong. Sign, Exponent and Mantissa is the IEEE 754 layout.

prompt: The revision exercise asks for zero, one, two and three address formats for which machine?
explanation: A Pentium 4 assembly language program segment. The other three machines all appear elsewhere in the course, which is what makes them plausible distractors.

why.a: Correct. A Pentium 4 assembly language program segment.
why.b: Wrong. The MC68000 supplies instruction examples in the ISA deck.
why.c: Wrong. The IBM 801 is an early RISC machine.
why.d: Wrong. DLX appears in the data hazard classification.

prompt: The revision exercise evaluates X equals A times B, plus C over D, all divided by F times G plus J times {{1}}.
explanation: K. The expression uses A, B, C, D, F, G, J and K, eight operands, which is why every version of the program is long.

prompt: In the revision worked answer, which instruction opens the three-address version?
explanation: MUL R1, A, B, because A times B is the innermost operation of the expression. DIV R2, C, D follows it.

why.a: Correct. MUL R1, A, B, because A times B is the innermost operation of the expression.
why.b: Wrong. It is the second instruction, not the first.
why.c: Wrong. It is the third, combining the first two results.
why.d: Wrong. PUSH belongs to the zero-address version.

prompt: The revision three-address answer ends with {{1}} X, R2, R3.
explanation: DIV, since the whole expression is one quantity divided by another, so the division is the last thing done.

prompt: How does the revision zero-address version begin?
explanation: Both operands are pushed before the operator, which is reverse Polish order. The program closes with POP X.

why.a: Correct. Both operands are pushed before the operator, which is reverse Polish order.
why.b: Wrong. MUL would find only one operand on the stack.
why.c: Wrong. MUL would find an empty stack.
why.d: Wrong. LOAD and a one-operand MUL belong to the one-address version.

prompt: The revision zero-address version ends with {{1}} X.
explanation: POP X, taking the single remaining value off the stack and writing it to X.
